name: Galantamine

lead: Galantamine is a prescription alkaloid originally from snowdrop plants, approved for mild to moderate Alzheimer disease. In nootropic circles it is used off-label for sharper thinking and more vivid dreams.
Research suggests it may increase dream recall and vividness, which is why it features in lucid-dreaming routines.

paras: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase, raising acetylcholine, and also acts at nicotinic receptors.
Common effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness and headache; serious ones include allergic reactions, stomach bleeding, liver injury and chest pain. It is Rx-only in the US and EU.

gallery.title: Galanthus nivalis L. Amaryllidaceae Snowdrop. Hardy, bulbous herb. Distribution: Europe. A chemical, galantamine, is sourced principally from the Caucasian snowdrop, Galanthus woronowii but is present in our ‘English’ snowdrop and related genera. It is a competitive, reversible, acetylcholinesterase inhibitor so increases brain acetylcholine, a chemical of great importance in cerebral function. As such it has been recommended for ameliorating the symptoms of mild to moderate Alzheimer’s disease, but not for mild cognitive impairment as in US clinical trials there was an increased mortality. Johnson (Gerard, 1633) calls it the bulbous violet, Viola theophrasti

chain: Users report sharper cognition and more vivid dreams
angle.text: People use it as a nootropic and a lucid-dreaming aid, linking mental performance and sleep quality to overall self-presentation. It is a prescription drug used off-label for these purposes.

lead: Galantamine is an alkaloid first isolated from snowdrop (Galanthus) and related Amaryllidaceae plants in the Soviet Union in the 1940s; it is now also made synthetically.[1] It is a prescription medicine for mild to moderate Alzheimer disease and works by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, raising acetylcholine levels.[1][2]

In nootropic and dream communities it is discussed for increasing dream vividness and recall, which can help people induce lucid dreams.[1] Interest in appearance is indirect: some users look to cognition, sleep and dream-related routines as part of a broader self-improvement approach.

paras: Galantamine is indicated for mild to moderate Alzheimer disease and vascular dementia, with limited success in more advanced dementia.[1] Reviews find that the efficacy of the three marketed cholinesterase inhibitors is similar and that the benefit is mild.[3]
It inhibits acetylcholinesterase and also acts at nicotinic receptors, although recent studies question whether it works as a positive allosteric modulator at some of them.[1]
Common effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness and headache. Serious risks include allergic reactions, stomach bleeding, liver injury and chest pain.[1]

Large randomized trials in Alzheimer disease were published in 2000.[4][5] A review of non-stimulant ADHD treatments reported negative findings for galantamine.[6] A pilot randomized trial examined safety in subarachnoid hemorrhage,[7] and randomized trials have examined cocaine use disorder and post-stroke aphasia.[8][9] Studies of its effect on lucid dreaming are described in general references.[1]
Galantamine is prescription-only in the US and EU.[1] The main brand name is Razadyne, and a derivative, benzgalantamine (Zunveyl), was FDA-approved in July 2024.[1]
